passages.original: sed rebellabunt pueri senibus, et ignobiles nobilibus, et mutuo corruent. Et implebitur illud Apostolicum : Mordentes invicem, consumpti estis ab invicem (Galat. v, 15). Hacc sub Tito tilio Vespasiani accidisse populo Judæorum, scribit Josephus (lib. v de Bello Jud.) : et quo'i, cnm expugnarentur a Romanis, fucril Jerusalem in tres partes divisa seditio : et alii arcem et templum, alii inferiorem, alii superiorem partem urbis tenuerint.
passages.english: but boys will rebel against old men, and the base-born against the noble, and they will fall upon one another. And that saying of the Apostle will be fulfilled: "Biting one another, you have been consumed by one another" (Gal. 5:15). Josephus writes (Jewish War, book 5) that these things happened to the Jewish people under Titus, the son of Vespasian: and that, when they were being besieged by the Romans, faction had divided Jerusalem into three parts, and some held the citadel and the temple, others the lower part of the city, others the upper.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected silently (Hacc = Haec, tilio = filio, quo'i cnm = quod cum, fucril = fuerit).

passages.original: ( VerSe 5, 4.) i Et ingrediantur portas duces : ego mandavi sactificatis meis, et vocavi fortes meos in ira mea exsul antes in gloria mea. > Principes, it g;g ,ntes juxta LXX Translatores Eusebius virtutes angelicas interpretatur, et pessimos dæmoi na, qui ad eversionem Babylonis missi sunt. Nos autem historiae ordinem prosequentes, Medos esse dicimus. De ciuibus in consequentibus apertius Scriptura tesatur, dicens : Ecce ego suscitabo su-per eos Medos, qui argentum non quaerant, nec aurum velint.
passages.english: (Verses 3–4.) "And let the leaders enter the gates: I have commanded my sanctified ones, and I have called my mighty ones in my wrath, exulting in my glory." Eusebius interprets the "princes," or "giants" according to the Seventy Translators, as angelic powers, and as the most wicked demons who were sent for the overthrow of Babylon. But we, following the order of the history, say that they are the Medes. Of whom Scripture testifies more openly in what follows, saying: "Behold, I will stir up against them the Medes, who do not seek silver nor desire gold."
passages.notes: The garbled "it g;g ,ntes" is read as "sive gigantes" ("or giants"), the Septuagint rendering; the verse reference is garbled in the scan ("5, 4"), probably 3–4.

passages.original: dicit Dominus exercituum. » Babylonem fuisse potentissimam, et in campestribus per quadrum sitam, abaugulo usque adangulum muri, sedecim, a millia tenuisse passuum, id est, simul per circuitum sexaginta quatuor, refert Herodotus 4,ei multi alii qui Græcas historias conscripserunt. Aix autem, id est, Capitolium illius urbis, est turris quae ædificata post diluvium, in altitudine quatuor millia dicitur tenere passuum I, paulatim de lato in angustias coarctata, ut pondus imminens facilius a lattoribus sustentetur.
passages.english: says the Lord of hosts." Herodotus and many others who wrote Greek histories relate that Babylon was most powerful, set on the plains in a square, and that its walls extended sixteen thousand paces from corner to corner, that is, sixty-four [thousand] all around. But the citadel, that is, the Capitol of that city, is the tower which was built after the Flood, and is said to reach four thousand paces in height, narrowed gradually from broad to narrow, so that the weight pressing down might be more easily supported by the sides.
passages.notes: "Aix" read as "Arx" (citadel); "lattoribus" read as "lateribus" (sides). Stray footnote marks omitted.

passages.original: aliis ex urbe fugientibus, aliis, quos hostis oppressit, vin- cutis alligatis. Sin autem ad Babyloniam captivitatem, quod et verius est, dicemus quod nou pugna, sed obsidione superati sint. Quod si in adventu Christi, juxta Eusebium, tropologice intelligere volueris: dices eos interfectos non gladio, sed infidelitate, omnesque principes eorum reces- sisse a Deo, et peccatorum funibus alligatos, lice quemquam fuisse de Pharisæis, qui non diaboli retibus alligatus sit.
passages.english: some fleeing from the city, others, whom the enemy overpowered, bound with chains. But if [you refer it] to the Babylonian captivity, which is also truer, we shall say that they were overcome not by battle but by siege. But if you wish to understand it tropologically of the coming of Christ, following Eusebius, you will say that they were slain not by the sword but by unbelief, and that all their princes withdrew from God and were bound with the cords of sins, and that there was not one of the Pharisees who was not bound in the nets of the devil.

passages.original: Quod autem Symmachus et TheoduLio λη̃μμα, id est, assumptionem semper interpretati sunt, hoc scire debemus, accepisse prophetam a Dommo gratiam spiritualem , ut Ægypti sacramenta cnguoscerel, sive oculis mentis aspiceret, ut LXX transtulerunt. NOli est autem Ægyptus ista quam Judæi putant, sicut arbitratus est Josephus, qui in libris Antiquitatum refert : Oniam sacerdotem Isaiæ implesse vaticinium, ut i in territorio Heliopolitano, quod Ægyplii 289 vo- μὸν vocant2, exstrueret templum ad similitudinem Templi Dei, et altare. Esto enim, concedamus hæc dicta lie Onia et altari quod in Ægypto exstruxit, quae erunt quinque civitates, quæ in Ægypto loquantur lingua Chanantica : ex quibus una juxta LXX appellatur 'Ασεδέϰ : juxta alios iuLerpretes, civitas ARS sive ARES, vel civitas solis ?
passages.english: As for the fact that Symmachus and Theodotion always rendered lēmma as "assumption" (taking up), we should understand this: that the prophet received from the Lord a spiritual grace, so that he might know the mysteries of Egypt, or see them with the eyes of the mind, as the Seventy translated. But this is not the Egypt that the Jews suppose, as Josephus thought, who relates in the books of the Antiquities that Onias the priest fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah, so that in the territory of Heliopolis, which the Egyptians call a nomos [district], he built a temple in the likeness of the Temple of God, and an altar. For suppose we grant that these things were said of Onias and the altar which he built in Egypt: what will be the five cities in Egypt that speak the Canaanite language, of which one according to the Seventy is called Asedek, and according to the other translators the city ARES or HERES, or the city of the sun?
passages.notes: "Ἀσεδέκ" as printed (LXX city of righteousness). Scanning errors (cnguoscerel = cognosceret, lie = de) corrected.

passages.original: » Consequenter ad id quod supra dixerat: In die illa erunt quinque civitates in terra Ægypti loquentes lingua Chana- nilide: et jurantes per Duminum exercituum, nunc infertur: Erit altare Domini in medio terræ Ægypti, quod Onias secundum Josephum (Antiqq. lib. XIII, cap. 6), male intelligens implere conatus est. Et titulus Domini continens passionem, in quo scri- ptum est Hebraicis litteris, Græcis, et Latinis : Jesus Nazarenus rex Judæorum (Juan.
passages.english: " In sequence with what he had said above, "In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the Canaanite language and swearing by the Lord of hosts," it is now added: "There will be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt," which Onias, according to Josephus (Antiquities book 13, chapter 6), misunderstanding it, tried to fulfil. And the "pillar of the Lord" [is] the inscription containing the passion, on which was written in Hebrew, Greek and Latin letters: "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews" (John
passages.notes: titulus means both "pillar/monument" (Isaiah's text) and "inscription" (on the cross); Jerome plays on both. Passage breaks off mid-reference (John 19:19).

passages.original: Quod quidem non Solum de haereticis, sed de omni potest intelligi peccatore, qui negligens peccata sua, desperatione tit pejor ; et voluptatibus irretitus, j un- git peccato blasphemiam, ut omnem 317 sensum viventium putet morte finiri, dicens illud Epicuri : < Post mortem nihit est, et mors ipsa nihil esL. »
passages.english: This indeed can be understood not only of heretics but of every sinner who, neglecting his sins, becomes worse through despair, and, entangled in pleasures, joins blasphemy to sin, so as to think that all the sensation of the living is ended by death, saying that saying of Epicurus: "After death there is nothing, and death itself is nothing."

passages.original: Non quod non interrogaverint, sed quod consilium propbetae 402 audire noluerint, sperantes auxilium in fortitudine Pharaonis, et habentes fiduciam in proiectione, sive umbra iEgypti. Pro fortitudine Pharaonis, quae in hoc luco bis ponitur, in Hebraico scriptum habet MAOZ (). Hoc adnotavimus, ut quod in Danielis extrema legimus (Dan. II) visione Deum MAOZIM (), non ut Porphyrius somniat, Deum viculi Modim [Al. Jloden], sed robustum Deum et fortem intelligamus. Pharao autem apud .Egyptios nomen est n giae potestatis; et unusquisque speciali appellatur vocabuło, ut Pharao Nechao, et Pharao Vafres [Al.
passages.english: Not that they did not ask, but that they were unwilling to hear the counsel of the prophet, hoping for help in the strength of Pharaoh, and having confidence in the protection, or shadow, of Egypt. For "strength of Pharaoh," which is set twice in this place, the Hebrew has MAOZ. We have noted this so that, where we read in the last vision of Daniel of the God MAOZIM, we may understand not, as Porphyry dreams, the god of the village of Modin, but the mighty and strong God. Pharaoh, moreover, among the Egyptians is the name of royal power; and each is called by a particular name, such as Pharaoh Necho and Pharaoh Vafres [other reading: Vafre]
passages.notes: "proiectione" probably for "protectione" (protection). "n giae" read as "regiae". Daniel reference printed as "Dan. II", likely Dan. 11. Hebrew script lost in the scan.

passages.original: Pugnasse autem Sennacherib regem Assyriorum contra Ægyptios, et obsedisse Ne usium, jamque exstructis aggeribus urbi capiendae, venisse Taracham regem iEthiopuv: in auxilium, et una nocte juxta Jerusalem centum Leviora (juycd.un infra emcu iaintis. octoginta quinque millia exercitus Assyrii pestilentia corruisse, narrat Herodotus, et plenissime Berosus 1, Chaldaicae scriptor historiæ, quorum fides de propriis libris petenda est.
passages.english: Herodotus relates, and most fully Berosus, the writer of Chaldean history, whose credibility must be sought from their own books, that Sennacherib king of the Assyrians fought against the Egyptians and besieged Pelusium, and that when mounds had already been built to take the city, Tarhaka king of the Ethiopians came to [its] aid, and that in one night near Jerusalem one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrian army fell by pestilence.
passages.notes: The text is corrupt: "Ne usium" read as Pelusium; the words "centum Leviora (juycd.un infra emcu iaintis." are garbled print, apparently intruded matter, and have been omitted except for "centum" (one hundred).

passages.original: Aiunt autem Hebræi hoc verbo significari tenuissimum pulverem, qui venio raptante saepe in oculos mittitur, et sentitur potius quam videtur. Minutissima erpo frusta puivcris et pene invisibilia, hoc verbo appellantur : quas forsian Democritus cum Epicuro suo atomos vocat. Multaque suut nomina quæ ita leguntur [Al. intelliliguntur] in Græco, ut in Hebraico posita suni, propter interpretandi difficultatem, ct ad compara- tionem linguæ Hebrææ, tam Græc. quam Latini sermonis pauperiem.
passages.english: The Hebrews say that this word signifies the finest dust, which, snatched up by the wind, is often thrown into the eyes and is felt rather than seen. The tiniest specks of dust, then, almost invisible, are called by this word; which perhaps Democritus with his Epicurus calls atoms. And there are many words which are read [other reading: understood] in Greek just as they are set down in Hebrew, because of the difficulty of translating, and because of the poverty of both Greek and Latin speech in comparison with the Hebrew language.

passages.original: Unde ad ipsum Cyrum Deus apostropham facit: Dedi tibi thesauros et absconditas opes cunctarum urbium; ut qui prius colebas idola, beneficiis unum sentires Deum, præsertim cum scias, multo antequam nascereris tuum nomen esse prædictum. Quod quidem et Josephus in undecimo Judaicae Antiquitatis volumine refert, legisse Cyrum ab Isaia de se certo vaticinatum nomine, et idcirco Judaeos quasi Dei familiares plurimum dilexisse. Haec autem, inquit, tribui libi propter Jacob servum meum, et lsrael electum meum, et vocavi te nomine tuo, sicut vocavi Abraham, Isaac et Jacob;
passages.english: Hence God makes an apostrophe to Cyrus himself: I have given you the treasures and hidden riches of all cities, so that you, who formerly worshipped idols, might through these benefits perceive the one God, especially since you know that your name was foretold long before you were born. Josephus too reports this in the eleventh book of the Jewish Antiquities: that Cyrus read that Isaiah had prophesied about him by his very name, and for that reason loved the Jews greatly, as being God's intimates. "These things," he says, "I have granted you for the sake of Jacob my servant and Israel my chosen, and I have called you by your name, as I called Abraham, Isaac and Jacob;

passages.original: Et propterea sciet, quia ipse qui prius locutus est per prophetas, præsens cru- diet populos. Juxta Septuaginta loquitur ad Israel Deus, quod in Ægyptum voluntate descenderit. Di- cente in Deuteronomio Moyse:In septuaginta anima- bus descenderunt patres tui in Ægyptum (Deut.I, 22) : et ab Assyriis captivi 605 violenter abdueti sunt. Unde dicitur ad eos ; Et nunc quid estis hic i quid facitis in terra Judæa, qui post necem prophetarum, in Dei Filium misisti manus ? Ant certe ad angelicas potestates, et præsides templi angelos loquitur Deus : Quid hie facitis, cur nou relinquitis populum blasphemantem ? quod et Josephus refert (lib. VI Antiq. Judaic. c. 12) ; apertis repente janu:s templi, et sponte reseratis, quas multi homines claudere vix poterant, vocem de adytis templi exisse disced- tium : Transeumus ex his sedibus.
passages.english: And therefore it will know that he who formerly spoke through the prophets will, being present, teach the peoples. According to the Septuagint, God speaks to Israel [saying] that it went down into Egypt of its own will, as Moses says in Deuteronomy: "With seventy souls your fathers went down into Egypt" (Deut. 10:22), whereas they were carried off violently as captives by the Assyrians. Hence it is said to them: "And now what are you [doing] here?" What are you doing in the land of Judaea, you who, after the slaughter of the prophets, laid hands on the Son of God? Or else God speaks to the angelic powers and to the angels who presided over the temple: "What are you doing here? Why do you not abandon a blaspheming people?" This Josephus also reports (Jewish Antiquities, book 6, ch. 12): that the doors of the temple suddenly opened and unbarred themselves of their own accord, doors which many men could scarcely close, and a voice came out of the inner sanctuary of the temple of those departing: "Let us pass over from these dwellings."
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected (erudiet, abducti, Aut, non, januis, discedentium, Transeamus). The Deuteronomy reference is printed as I, 22; the verse is 10:22. The Josephus citation as printed (Antiquities 6) is doubtful; the episode belongs to the Jewish War, book 6.

passages.original: De quo et in hoc codeta Propheta legitur, Erit radix Jesse : et quiresurget ut principetur gentium, in ipso gentes sperabunt (Isa. XI, 10). Isti autem plurimi quondam a fortibus tenebantur ; et sub specie asinae et pulli, multos habebant dominos, quibus dixerum apostoli : Dominus eos necessarios habet (Matth. XXI, 5). Qui fortes erant antequam Christus humanum corpus assumeret, et forte superato, diriperet domum ejus. Prædam ergo fortium apostolis suis tradidit alqne divisit, ut Petrus, Jacobus, et 623 Joannes, circumcisi populi principes fierent, et Paulus et Barnabas mitterentur ad gentes, locis, non animo separati, et suh uno Domino in diversa starent acie, III agminis utriusque victoria, triumphum erigerent Salvatori. Ex quo qui dispensatoriam inter Petrum et Paulum COIUtIlDlio- nem (Act. xvj, verc dicunt jurgium fuisse atque certamen, ut blasphemanti Porphyrio satisfaciant : et veteris legis caeremonias in Ecclesia Christi, a stirpe credentis Israel asserunt esse servandas, de- Lent et auream in mille annis exspectare JcrusalenJ, ut victimas ilUluolenl, et circumcidautur, ut in Sah- Lato sedeant, dorluianl, saturentur, inebrientur, et surgant ludere, qui ludus offendit Deum.
passages.english: Of him it is also read in this same prophet: "There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who shall rise to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope" (Isa. 11:10). These many were once held by the strong, and under the figure of the she-ass and the colt they had many masters, to whom the apostles said: "The Lord has need of them" (Matt. 21). These [masters] were strong before Christ took on a human body and, having overcome the strong one, plundered his house. So he handed over and divided the spoil of the strong among his apostles. Thus Peter, James and John became leaders of the people of the circumcision, and Paul and Barnabas were sent to the gentiles, separated in place, not in mind. Under one Lord they stood in different battle lines, so that by the victory of both columns they might raise a triumph to the Saviour. Hence those who say that the arranged dispute (dispensatoria communio?) between Peter and Paul (Acts 15) was truly a quarrel and a contest, so as to satisfy the blaspheming Porphyry, and who assert that the ceremonies of the old law must be kept in the Church of Christ by those of the stock of believing Israel, ought also to await a golden Jerusalem for a thousand years. There they would offer victims and be circumcised, sit idle on the Sabbath, sleep, eat their fill, get drunk, and rise up to play, a play which offends God.
passages.notes: The word printed "COIUtIlDlio- nem" is garbled; probably "contentionem" (dispute), hence "arranged dispute", or "communionem". "III" read as "ut". "Sedeant" (sit idle) is uncertain. The Acts reference is garbled (xvj); the Matthew verse is given as 21:5 but the quotation is 21:3.

passages.original: Et per hanc occasionem, multaque hujuscemodi, Hispaniarum et niaxime Lusitaniæ deceptae sunt mulierculæ, oneratae peccatis, quae ducuntur desideriis variis, semper discentes, et nunquam ad scientiam veritatis pervenientes (11 Tin. II,), ut Basilidis, Balsami atque Thesauris, Barhelonis quoque et Leusiboræ, ac reliquorum nominum portenta susciperent. Dequi- Lus diligentissime vir apostolicus scribit IrenaeuS, episcopus Lugdunensis et martyr, multarum origines explicans haereseon, et maxime Gnosticorum, qui per Marcum Ægyptium, Galliarum primum circa Rhodanum, deindc Hispaniarum nobiles feminas deceperunt, miscentes fabulis voluptatem, et impe- ritiæ suae nomen scientiæ vindicantes (Irenæus, lib.
passages.english: On this pretext, and many others of the kind, the silly women of the Spanish provinces, and especially of Lusitania, were deceived: women laden with sins, led by various desires, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth (2 Tim. 3). As a result they took up the monstrosities of Basilides, Balsamus and Thesaurus, and also of Barbelo and Leusibora, and of the remaining names. Of these the apostolic man Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons and martyr, writes most diligently, setting out the origins of many heresies. He deals especially with the Gnostics, who through Mark the Egyptian deceived noble women, first of the Gauls around the Rhône, then of the Spains, mixing pleasure with fables and claiming the name of knowledge for their ignorance (Irenaeus, book
passages.notes: Balsamus, Thesaurus and Leusibora are obscure Gnostic names; "Barhelonis" read as Barbelo. The Timothy reference is garbled in the print (2 Tim. 3:6–7). The final citation is cut off.

passages.original: Nos autem juxta e.t quæ ex pers ona Salvatoris sequuntur : Apparui his qui non interrogabant. Inventus sum ab his qni me non quærebant (Isa. LXV, I) ; ad tempus Romanæ victoriae universa referimus, quæ Josephus Judaicæ scriptor historiæ, septem explicat voluminibus, qnibus imposuit titulum Captivitatis Judaicæ, id est Περί ὰλώσεως : et superfluum est ea sermone dis- . serere, quæ oculis pateant, cum omnia desiderat - bilia eorum versa sint in ruinas, et templum in .
passages.english: We, however, in keeping also with what follows in the person of the Saviour, "I appeared to those who did not ask for me; I was found by those who did not seek me" (Isa. 65:1), refer all these things to the time of the Roman victory. Josephus, the historian of the Jews, sets this out in seven volumes, to which he gave the title The Jewish Captivity, that is, Peri haloseos. It is superfluous to discourse in words on things that lie open to the eyes, since all their desirable things have been turned into ruins, and the temple, [once]
passages.notes: The sentence is cut off and continues in the following passage. The Greek title means "On the Capture".

passages.original: » LXX : « Et ego opera corum, et cogitationes eorum novi, ct venio congregare omnes gentes et omnes linguas : et venient et videbunt gloriam meam, et dimittam super eos signum : et emittam ex eis, qui salvati fuerint ad gentes, in Tharsis et Phud, et Lud et Mosoch et Thobel, et in Graciam, et in insulas longe, qui non audierunt nomen meum, neque viderunt gloriam rocam. » Priusquam exponam quid significet enumeratio gentium plurimarum, breviter de interpretationis varietate dicendum est. Tharsis lingua Hebrxa 2 , mare appellatur ; et ( ut aiunt) Indiae regio : licet Josephus, littera commutata, Tarsum putct nuncupari pro Tharsis, urbem Ciliciae, ad quam Jonas de Joppe fugiens, ire cupiebat (Jonæ I). Phud autem, sivc Phul, Libyes, omnisque Africa usque ad mare Mauritaniæ, in qua 817 fluvius hodie qui Phud dicitur, ct cuncta circa eum regio Phulensis appellatur.
passages.english: LXX: "And I know their works and their thoughts, and I come to gather all nations and all tongues; and they shall come and see my glory. And I will send upon them a sign, and I will send out from them those who have been saved to the nations, to Tharsis and Phud and Lud and Mosoch and Thobel, and to Greece, and to the distant islands, who have not heard my name nor seen my glory." Before I explain what the listing of so many nations signifies, something must briefly be said about the variety of the translations. In the Hebrew language Tharsis means the sea, and also (as they say) a region of India. Josephus, however, changing a letter, thinks that Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, is meant by Tharsis; this was where Jonah, fleeing from Joppa, wished to go (Jonah 1). Phud, or Phul, is Libya and all Africa as far as the Mauretanian sea. In it there is today a river called Phud, and the whole region around it is called Phulensis.
passages.notes: "rocam" read as "meam"; "Graciam" as "Græciam". The final clause is grammatically loose in the Latin.
